step1.title: Take the Challenge
step1.heading: Make the sign. Film it.
step1.body: Open your camera. Face it toward you. Make the Butterfly Sign — hands on heart, open like wings. No filter. No production. Just you, showing up for someone.
step1.tip: Hold a name in your mind. You don't have to say it out loud.

step2.title: Show the Love
step2.heading: Say their name.
step2.body: Look into the camera and say: "I see you. I care. You're not alone." Or: "I got you, [name]." Say their name out loud. That's what makes it real.
step2.tip: This isn't a script. Say whatever is true.

step3.title: Lift 3 More
step3.heading: Tag 3 people. Pass it forward.
step3.body: Nominate 3 people you care about. Give them 24 hours. One becomes three becomes nine becomes a billion. That's the butterfly effect.
step3.tip: They don't need followers. They need one person to think of.

step1.instruction: Place both hands on your heart.

step2.detail: Right over left, thumbs hooked together.

step3.detail: Spread your fingers wide. That's the Butterfly Sign.

music.name: Music
music.detail: Music reaches where words stop. 1 billion people carry something in silence. That silence has never had a sound. Until now.

dance.name: Dance
dance.detail: Dance turns emotion into motion. Every movement that lived in the body outlasted every movement that lived only in the mind.

fashion.name: Fashion

art.name: Art

faith.name: Faith

story.heroSub: From a moment of crisis in 1998 to a global movement in 2026.

origin.label: The Origin
origin.title: 1998 · Hurricane Pauline
origin.imgAlt: Lucina Artigas guiding survivors through the butterfly hug after Hurricane Pauline
origin.p1: Lucina Artigas was a therapist in Mexico when Hurricane Pauline devastated the coast. In the aftermath, thousands of people — many of them children — were in severe psychological trauma with nowhere to turn.
origin.p2: She created a simple bilateral stimulation gesture anyone could do without a therapist present. Two hands crossed on your chest, alternating taps. She called it the butterfly hug.

spread.label: Global Adoption
spread.title: 2000–2024 · The Spread
spread.p: The butterfly hug moved through disaster zones, refugee camps, and crisis centers globally. It became embedded in EMDR therapy, in NGO protocols, in first responder training. It worked. It was simple. It was free. And it didn't require permission.

tipping.label: The Tipping Point
tipping.title: May 2024 · The Moment
tipping.imgAlt: The butterfly hug demonstrated on a global stage
tipping.p: Prince Harry demonstrated the butterfly hug on stage. It was seen by millions. Suddenly, the gesture wasn't hidden in clinical papers anymore. It was visible. It was real. And it belonged to everyone.

challenge.label: This Moment
challenge.title: April 2026 · The Challenge
challenge.p: We're organizing the first coordinated global moment. One night. One gesture. Visible proof that mental health care is a human right, not a luxury. That you can lead change without permission.

cta.title: You're part of this story.
cta.sub: It started with one person helping another. Join the next chapter.

science.heroSub: The neuroscience behind the butterfly hug — backed by research, used by therapists worldwide.

brain.label: How Your Brain Works
brain.title: Crossing the midline.
brain.p1: When you perform the butterfly hug — alternating stimulation across your body's midline — you activate both hemispheres of your brain simultaneously. Your left side notices movement on the right. Your right notices movement on the left.
brain.p2: This bilateral stimulation is how your brain processes and integrates overwhelming information. It's the same mechanism that happens during REM sleep, when your eyes move side-to-side. It helps your nervous system work through stress.

emdr.label: Clinical Foundation
emdr.title: Built on EMDR science.
emdr.imgAlt: Butterfly hug gesture with calming ripples
emdr.p1: Dr. Francine Shapiro developed EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) therapy in the late 1980s. She discovered that bilateral eye movements, combined with processing traumatic memories, helped people heal from PTSD. Since then, EMDR has become a WHO-recommended treatment for post-traumatic stress.
emdr.p2: Lucina Artigas adapted this science. Instead of eye movements guided by a therapist, she created a self-soothing version: two hands, bilateral stimulation, no therapist needed. The butterfly hug puts clinical neuroscience in your own hands.

neuro.label: The Evidence
neuro.title: What brain scans show.
neuro.imgAlt: Brain scan showing prefrontal cortex activation
neuro.p1: fMRI studies of people using bilateral stimulation show reduced activation in the amygdala — the part of your brain that triggers fear and anxiety. At the same time, activity increases in the prefrontal cortex, the part that helps you think clearly, make rational decisions, and feel safe.
neuro.p2: In plain language: the butterfly hug tells your alarm system to stand down. It doesn't make the threat go away. It helps your brain recognize that, right now, in this moment, you can breathe.

quote.text: The butterfly hug is not therapy. It's what humans do instinctively when someone is hurting. Now we know why it works.
quote.attribution: — Clinical neuroscience literature on bilateral stimulation

disclaimer.text: The butterfly hug is a grounding tool, not a replacement for therapy. If you're struggling with trauma, depression, or suicidal thoughts, please talk to a professional.
disclaimer.label: Important Clarification
disclaimer.title: This is not therapy.
disclaimer.p1: The butterfly hug is evidence-based. It's used by therapists. But performing the gesture is not the same as therapy. It's a tool. A gesture. A moment where your nervous system can find a little more calm.
disclaimer.p2: But for the everyday moments when you're stressed, overwhelmed, or need to ground yourself? The science says: try it. Your brain will thank you.
